global.headline: QATAR PUTS NUCLEAR INSPECTIONS INTO THE HORMUZ BARGAIN AS WASHINGTON STRIKES AGAIN AND BIDS $20 MILLION FOR WHAT IT CALLS DESTROYED
summary: The Qatari proposal now trades the Strait of Hormuz for the nuclear file rather than deferring it. Under terms reported on Saturday, Washington would lift the naval blockade, end oil sanctions and release about US$8 billion of frozen Iranian money; Tehran would admit IAEA inspectors to the nuclear facilities struck by US and Israeli bombs, and reopen the strait on the second day of a two-stage, 48-hour sequence, using a route coordinated with Oman and jointly registered with the International Maritime Organisation. No agreement has been reached, and neither government has rejected it.

Trump said the United States had carried out fresh "minor strikes" on Iran after two missiles hit Qeshm Island; Iranian state media said a US MQ-9 drone was shot down over the island on Saturday. The State Department's Rewards for Justice programme offered up to US$20 million for information on Iran's nuclear facilities, equipment and scientists — awkwardly beside Trump's claim that the programme was obliterated. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned on Wednesday against "the slightest inclination towards submission", and Mohsen Rezaei, whose seven conditions of 3 November remain unanswered, wrote that Iran had defeated Trump on the battlefield, in the strait and in Washington. Brent's last settlement before the weekend was US$98.32 and WTI US$90.83, closing a fall of about 13 per cent, the worst week since 2022.
global.geopolitical: Deferring the nuclear file was the original MOU's central device; folding inspections of bombed sites into the price of the strait abandons it and makes verification the thing Iran sells — exactly what its hardliners call submission.
global.socioeconomic: A 13 per cent weekly fall in crude the war itself created shows the market now treats a deal as likelier than another offensive — relief that reaches pumps and freight only if the second day arrives.

global.headline: HERZOG HANDS THE MANDATE TO EISENKOT, AND NETANYAHU LOSES THE FIRST ATTEMPT
summary: President Isaac Herzog announced on Saturday that he will task Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, the former armed forces chief, with forming Israel's next government, with the formal ceremony on Sunday. Factions holding 67 Knesset seats recommended Eisenkot, 46 recommended Benjamin Netanyahu and one faction of seven recommended nobody. Eisenkot has 28 days, extendable by 14; if he fails, Herzog must decide within three days whether to pass the mandate on, probably to Netanyahu.

The arithmetic is worse than the recommendations suggest. The 67 includes the Arab-led parties, which won a record 19 seats on 27 October and with whom Eisenkot has ruled out sitting — leaving him 48, thirteen short. Neither Bennett's nor Liberman's party has committed to joining or guaranteeing confidence, though he could govern with fewer than 61 seats if he survives the vote. Netanyahu, who claims the mandate on Likud's 27 seats, had his fraud claims rejected by the election commission.
global.geopolitical: The prime minister who has run the war since February would be replaced mid-negotiation by the general who commanded the army before it, just as Washington weighs Tehran's terms — a change of Israeli signature on anything Qatar brokers.
global.socioeconomic: Four weeks of caretaker government arrive with US$4 billion of American military aid due to stop on 31 December, so those budget decisions fall to whoever wins a confidence vote, not the outgoing cabinet.

global.headline: RUSSIA TAKES OUT KYIV'S POWER AND WATER WITH 36 BALLISTIC MISSILES DAYS BEFORE THE ABU DHABI TALKS
summary: Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, of which Ukraine's air force intercepted four, alongside 172 drones, 149 of them downed. The energy ministry said strikes on facilities outside the capital, including the systems carrying power from two nuclear plants into the city, caused serious damage; the regional governor reported hits in at least three districts. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said missiles struck the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro and that heating and water were disrupted as well as electricity; water pressure was later stabilised. Moscow said it had targeted military-industrial, energy and transport infrastructure.

Zelensky said Russia was preparing for the trilateral talks by firing ballistic missiles at critical infrastructure. The US-led Russia-Ukraine round in Abu Dhabi is due next week, and the strike follows another large wave on 5 November that the grid operator called one of the year's worst.
global.geopolitical: Four interceptions out of thirty-six is the operative fact of the Abu Dhabi round: Moscow can turn off a capital city on the eve of talks and Kyiv cannot stop it, which prices every guarantee Zelensky is offered.
global.socioeconomic: Three million people in Kyiv enter the cold months with power, heat and water hanging on substations two nuclear plants feed through, on top of the scheduled blackouts already running nationwide.

global.headline: NEW ZEALAND'S ELECTION ENDS WITHOUT A WINNER AND A THREE-WEEK-OLD PARTY HOLDS THE BALANCE
summary: Neither bloc won Saturday's general election outright. The preliminary count put Christopher Luxon's National-led coalition with ACT and NZ First at 67 or 68 of a projected 131 seats, against a 66-seat majority, with Luxon calling it too close to call while claiming a pathway to govern. Qiulae Wong's Opportunity Party took about 6 per cent of the party vote and a provisional seven seats, enough to decide the government from outside either bloc.

Between roughly 399,000 and 700,000 special votes are uncounted, about 14 per cent of the total, and they have historically favoured the left. The official result is not due until 27 November, with the coalition governing as caretaker until then. Both major parties lost share to minor parties.
global.geopolitical: A Five Eyes government sits in caretaker limbo for three weeks over AUKUS Pillar II and its China trade balance, with the deciding votes held by a party that has never sat in parliament.
global.socioeconomic: Caretaker convention blocks any new fiscal decision in an economy that has been in and out of recession, and a hung parliament makes whatever budget follows a negotiated document rather than a programme.

global.headline: A DRUG CUT INHERITED CHOLESTEROL RISK BY 78 PER CENT AND CHANGED NOTHING, COLLAPSING CARDIOLOGY'S BIGGEST BET
summary: Novartis's pelacarsen lowered lipoprotein(a) by about 78 per cent over 4.7 years in the phase 3 Lp(a)HORIZON trial and did not reduce heart attacks, strokes or cardiovascular death: the primary endpoint occurred in 12.3 per cent of patients on the drug against 12.1 per cent on placebo, in roughly 8,300 people with existing cardiovascular disease and high Lp(a). Adverse events were more common on the drug. Cleveland Clinic ran the trial, presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions in Chicago and published in the New England Journal of Medicine; researchers described themselves as stunned.

It was the meeting's second failure. Novo Nordisk's ziltivekimab, an interleukin-6 inhibitor, also missed in the phase 3 ZEUS trial — major cardiovascular events in 17.6 per cent against 17.7 per cent on placebo, a hazard ratio of 0.99, despite confirmed falls in IL-6 and hsCRP — with more serious infections on the drug. Lp(a) is genetically determined, unaffected by statins and raised in a fifth of the population; Amgen, Eli Lilly and Merck still have outcome trials running.
global.geopolitical: Two decades of genetic epidemiology pointed at Lp(a) and inflammation as the next targets after LDL; both hypotheses failed on the same stage in one week, resetting what regulators and national screening programmes can be asked to fund.
global.socioeconomic: Lowering a number in the blood is not the same as preventing an event, and the people who feel it are the one in five adults told an inherited risk would soon be treatable, who now have statins and blood-pressure control and nothing else.

singapore.headline: SM LEE TELLS AUSTRALIA TO BUY ITSELF ROOM BY GOING DEEPER INTO SOUTHEAST ASIA, NOT BY PICKING A SIDE
summary: Delivering the ABC's Boyer Lecture, "Engaging Asia from Down Under", Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong argued that Australia should deepen its economic, security and people-to-people ties with Southeast Asia to strengthen its own competitiveness and resilience in a fragmented world, and that doing so would give it more room to pursue its own interests amid US-China rivalry. He urged Australian businesses to invest more in ASEAN economies, said Australia should maintain its defence presence in the region, and pressed it to keep contact and pragmatic working arrangements with countries where relations are more complicated.

He framed the aim as helping countries "see each other as partners in development, and not solely through the prism of US-China rivalry". The lecture closes the ABC's 2026 series on Australia-Asia engagement.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is making the hedging case to the ally most exposed to it: an Australia with its own stake in Southeast Asia is a second voice against regional alignment choices, worth more to Singapore than any bilateral agreement.
singapore.socioeconomic: Australian capital is under-invested in ASEAN relative to its trade with China, and the practical ask — direct investment and a sustained defence presence — pays Singapore whichever way Washington turns after January.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE'S BANKS ARE TOLD THE EASY YEARS ARE OVER AND 2027 WILL HAVE TO BE EARNED
summary: Analysts told CNA that the three local banks face a tougher 2027 despite the prospect of higher interest rates, because the boom years did the work for them and growth must now be generated internally. DBS was called the steadiest: management says net interest income has bottomed and expects mid-single-digit total income growth next year, with its third-quarter miss traced to markets trading income. UOB's difficulties were described as structural, with thinner margins and costs still rising. OCBC posted third-quarter net profit of S$2.04 billion, up 3 per cent and ahead of estimates, expects low double-digit loan growth this year and says it is well placed for higher rates, though Great Eastern makes group earnings lumpier when bond markets move sharply. The assessment lands a day after the AI sell-off hit Singapore tech stocks, read as a correction rather than the end of the boom.
singapore.geopolitical: The banks' margin story now runs through the Middle East: the Bank of England raised rates this week citing conflict-driven energy costs, and that inflation path, not local loan demand, decides whether higher-for-longer helps or hurts them.
singapore.socioeconomic: The three are over half the Straits Times Index and the core of most Singaporean portfolios and CPF equity exposure, so a year of manufacturing growth rather than collecting it is a dividend question for households.

singapore.headline: AN OFFSHORE BETTING SITE IS STILL RENTING SINGAPORE SHELL COMPANIES AND BILLING THE BETS AS SECOND-HAND GAMING GEAR
summary: A Straits Times investigation found that Curacao-based GemBet still recruits people in Singapore to register shell companies and issue fake invoices so that bets look like ordinary purchases, four months after the arrangement was first exposed. One invoice billed S$80 for pre-owned gaming equipment from a Singapore-registered company operating out of a Punggol residential address; choosing PayNow routes a bettor's money through one of these firms rather than to the site. Nine people have previously been arrested over the site. GemBet, said to be run by a syndicate with links to Cyprus, calls the local firms legitimate affiliates and will not say how much of its money comes from Singapore.
Singapore Pools is the only licensed operator for lotteries, sports betting and remote gambling; betting with an unlawful operator carries a fine of up to S$10,000, six months' jail, or both.
singapore.geopolitical: The structure works because a Singapore company registration and a PayNow handle read abroad as evidence of legitimacy, making the ease of incorporating here an export of reputational cover rather than an enforcement problem.
singapore.socioeconomic: The people exposed are the mules, who sign for companies and invoices in their own names for a fee while the operator keeps its distance; nine arrests have not changed the economics of recruiting the next ten.

singapore.headline: UNPAID WORKERS ARE MATCHED WITH NEW EMPLOYERS WHILE THEIR CLAIMS ARE STILL OPEN, AND THE CASELOAD HAS DOUBLED
summary: More than 230 migrant workers, mostly Bangladeshi, were interviewed by construction and process firms at a job-matching session on 6 November at the Manpower Ministry's onboarding centre in Sengkang West, where they are temporarily housed while their October salary claims remain pending. They come from two process-sector companies under ministry investigation for unpaid wages, Process Maintenance Solutions and Jurong Technical & Construction. Some have been paid: a source at one firm said nearly all of its roughly 120 affected workers had received their back pay. The Migrant Workers' Centre would not say where the claims stand.

The number of workers reporting unpaid wages to the centre has doubled in the first ten months of 2026 against the same period in both 2024 and 2025. NTUC and the centre have rolled out financial aid alongside the job support.
singapore.geopolitical: Bangladesh's labour-sending ministries watch these cases closely because recruitment debt is incurred before departure, and a doubling of wage claims in Singapore is an argument in every bilateral talk on placement fees.
singapore.socioeconomic: Housing claimants at a government centre and finding them employers before the claims resolve keeps men earning instead of waiting, but the test is whether the two firms pay, not whether the workers are re-employed.

singapore.headline: SMRT ASKS COMMUTERS TO STAND ON BOTH SIDES OF THE ESCALATOR AND FINDS THEM UNWILLING
summary: A month-long trial that began on 29 October at City Hall and Raffles Place asks commuters to stand on both sides of escalators and hold the handrail, announced over station speakers and on new signage. SMRT Trains president Lam Sheau Kai said the aim is to cut slips, trips and falls while testing whether filling both sides of each step uses capacity more efficiently. Observations on 6 and 7 November found most commuters still standing on the left and walking up on the right, and all ten commuters CNA interviewed preferred the existing convention: at City Hall those who walked took about 20 seconds against 30 for those standing. Transport for London's comparable Holborn trial reported capacity gains of up to 30 per cent but could not stop passengers drifting back to a walking lane.
singapore.geopolitical: Not foreign policy, but a clean test of persuasion in a system that usually legislates — the instrument Singapore is relying on for social-media use and sodium labelling, measured against a thirty-year habit.
singapore.socioeconomic: Escalator falls are a rising cost in a country that entered its super-aged year in 2026, and the trial sets one commuter's 10 seconds against the station's throughput.

word.definition: A secondary phenomenon that accompanies or arises from another process without causing it.
word.etymology: From Greek epi-, "upon, in addition", and phainomenon, "thing appearing", from phainesthai, "to appear"; adopted in nineteenth-century medicine for symptoms incidental to a disease, and later in philosophy of mind.
word.example: Cutting lipoprotein(a) by 78 per cent without preventing a single extra heart attack suggests the particle may be an epiphenomenon of cardiovascular risk rather than a cause of it.
